items.summary: Coordinated multi-humanoid loco-manipulation is promising yet challenging due to high-dimensional whole-body control, decentralized decision making, and scalability. While recent reinforcement learning methods have improved single-humanoid whole-body control, extending them to the multi-humanoid setting remains nontrivial and often requires substantial reward engineering or task-specific design. We propose MASkillBlender, a general multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to achieve decentralized multi-humanoid whole-body coordination. By learning a shared decentralized high-level policy over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills, MASkillBlender enables coordinated behaviors using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references. To improve learning efficiency, we further introduce a permutation-based data augmentation strategy for homogeneous multi-humanoid systems, and theoretically show that the permuted samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples under the homogeneous Markov game formulation. We evaluate MASkillBlender on multiple multi-humanoid coordination tasks across two humanoid embodiments. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves strong task performance and enables coordinated behaviors across different tasks and humanoid embodiments.
items.title: MASkillBlender: Decentralized Whole-Body Coordination for Multi-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Skill Blending

items.summary: Multi-agent AI scientists have shown improving performance across a diverse range of tasks. Yet a common approach is design-time agentic orchestration, which typically relies on fixed workflows. In contrast, human scientists coordinate and adjust their division of labor at runtime. We therefore ask: can AI scientists also coordinate at runtime? To this end, we introduce Runtime Agent Coordination (RAC), which selects agents from existing AI-scientist hosts during execution, assigns scoped work contracts, and provides artifact-grounded verification. Verification informs subsequent agents without blocking transitions or discarding artifacts. We conduct a single-seed exploratory evaluation across Agent Laboratory, EvoScientist, and ARK on ResearchClawBench, preserving host models, tools, and permissions under host-calibrated budgets. Four cumulative conditions separate native execution, runtime communication, runtime selection, and the combined addition of contracts and verification. Runtime selection yields the highest observed mean score for each host; adding contracts and verification reduces these means, with host-dependent outcomes relative to native execution. These results motivate runtime coordination while exposing the limits of additional coordination mechanisms under constrained budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/systemind-team/Runtime-AI-Scientist.
items.title: Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23121305 . This narrative review asks how psychosexual rehabilitation after cancer can be delivered at scale, rather than describing how common sexual dysfunction is. The author organizes the intervention evidence by intensity of care. Low-intensity measures (structured discussion, lubricants and moisturizers, topical lidocaine, brief clinician training) are cheap and reasonably supported. Two widely recommended physical interventions have weaker evidence than assumed: scheduled PDE5 inhibitor "penile rehabilitation" and routine vaginal dilation during radiotherapy. Psychological interventions show small pooled effects, but moderate effects in targeted trials, most clearly therapist-guided internet-based CBT in breast cancer. From this the author proposes a five-step stepped-care model (Steps 0–4, built on extended PLISSIT) with explicit criteria for stepping up and down, plus adaptations for AYA, men on ADT, and sexual and gender minority survivors. The paper moves the field forward by reframing the problem as one of delivery, by challenging two entrenched practices, and by turning scattered evidence into a model that oncology teams, including nurses, could adopt and test. Major issues Methods are not reproducible. The review relies on "targeted searches" with no databases, dates, search terms, or selection process described. Evidence is "appraised qualitatively" with no tool such as GRADE or risk-of-bias assessment. Claims like "strongest trial evidence in breast cancer" may reflect selective sampling. The stepped-care model is not empirically validated. It was derived by the author "mapping" interventions to levels of care, with no consensus process, stakeholder input, or implementation data. The 8–12 week step-up threshold has no cited support. The conclusion that evidence "supports matching intensity to need" goes beyond what the cited studies tested, since none compared stepped care with usual care or direct referral (the paper admits this only at the end). Evidence for Steps 0–2 is mostly clinician-level, not patient-level. The cited training studies show clinicians discuss sexuality more often, not that patient outcomes improve. Yet these steps form the base of the model. Feasibility of nurse- or clinician-delivered care also rests largely on one HSCT trial. Key claims rest on weak or non-peer-reviewed sources. The HSCT multimodal trial [34] is a conference abstract that is called "important for the model." Other supports [28, 47] are also abstracts. Pilot RCTs (23 and 29 couples) underpin the "medium-to-large" couple therapy claims. The paper applies evidence standards inconsistently. It criticizes penile rehabilitation and during-radiotherapy dilation for weak evidence, then recommends supported dilation after radiotherapy based on observational data and an uncontrolled 53-woman cohort (11.5% to 60.9% pre-post), and cites a regimen from an abstract [28]. Inference from pooled versus targeted effects is speculative. The difference (SMD 0.24 vs. d 0.43–0.72) is taken to show that interventions work best when targeted, which supports stepped care. It could equally reflect heterogeneity, study quality, outcome measures, or small-study effects. Effect sizes of different metrics are also compared without confidence intervals. There is no limitations section. It should cover search bias, the breast-cancer skew, scarce data for men, SGM, and LMIC settings, and the lack of cost and workforce evidence. Minor issues PLISSIT is never spelled out, and AYA HOPE is not defined. "Psychosexual rehabilitation" is defined as a staged process but used loosely to include medical and physical treatments. A tighter definition would help. Table 2 level-of-care labels are confusing ("Steps 0–2", "Step 2 (on-demand use)" for a scheduled intervention). The HSCT row gives no sample size. Table 2 says the CBT

items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). items.summary: Berggren's three matrices generate the tree of primitive Pythagorean triples and preserve the quadratic form x₁² + x₂² − x₃². Cha, Nguyen and Tauber (2018) built such trees for other integral ternary forms Q of signature (2,1). We ask whether the matrices alone determine Q. Main results: Recovery criterion (Theorem 3.1). A set of isometries of Q determines Q up to scale exactly when no nonzero vector is sent to plus or minus itself by all of them. Equivalently, the group they generate is not virtually abelian; for integral isometries, it acts irreducibly. The proof is elementary linear algebra and applies to arbitrary real groups. Berggren trees (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Remark 3.5). Any two generators determine Q in Berggren's tree and in each of the five trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber. The definition of a Berggren tree alone does not force this: the generators A and A² give a Berggren forest for x₁² + x₂² − x₃² whose two generators both yield edges but do not determine Q. Roots at a rational null line (Theorem 3.6). For a primitive null vector P with divisor G, the minimum of Q on (P^⊥ ∩ ℤ³) \ ℤP is S = |det(2J)|/(2G²). An explicit congruence, Gm ≡ −τ (mod S), decides which minimal vectors e + mP are roots. N-cusps (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Corollary 3.9). For Q = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂² − Nx₃² with D = b² − 4ac < 0, all data at the null vectors (p, q, 1) are explicit. A minimal root exists there if and only if gcd(G, S) divides D/G, and in particular whenever D is cube-free. Recovery by integral reflections (Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13). Minimal roots at two or three distinct rational null lines yield three integral reflections that determine Q. The paper also relates the reflections in the trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber to minimal roots (Remark 3.17), and states an open question for trees produced by their construction.
items.title: The Inverse Berggren Tree Problem

items.summary: Language functions not only as a means of transmitting information but also as a repository of cultural knowledge, collective experience, and culturally shaped patterns of thought. Consequently, translation involves more than the transfer of lexical and grammatical information between languages. It also requires the interpretation and reconstruction of meanings that are embedded within particular cultural contexts. This issue becomes especially evident in the translation of idioms, proverbs, metaphors, realia, and other culture-specific expressions whose meanings cannot always be derived from their individual lexical components. In Translation Studies, such elements are commonly discussed as culture-specific items (CSIs), which may require particular strategies to preserve their semantic, pragmatic, and cultural dimensions in the target language (Aixelá, 1996).
tags: Idiomatic expressions provide a particularly clear illustration of the relationship between language and culture.

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). items.summary: Abstract We present a comprehensive, universal, abstract group-theoretic, module-theoretic, and category-theoretic formalization of bijectively separated rank arithmetic . Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Furthermore, when lane outputs collapse into a single target background group H, we isolate the exact relation subgroup KP =ker(ΨP) and prove the quotient isomorphism A(P)/KP∼= ⟨P1, . . . , Pr⟩ ≤ H, measuring the precise algebraic information lost during scalar collapse. Finally, we formulate the extension to infinite complex power orbits , polynomial root reconstruction via Newton symmetrization of ranked power arrays Pr ∈ Cr×r, Chinese Remainder Theorem grid decompositions over composite moduli, native linear rank complexity bounds Θ(m), and an axiomatic minimal proof assistant kernel . Keywords: Abstract algebra, cyclic groups, direct products, exponent coordinates, re- lation lattices, projection functors, natural transformations, Newton identities, Chinese Remainder Theorem, rank complexity. items.summary: GradLint is a fast, standalone Rust-based command-line tool and Python package for diffusion MRI gradient-table quality control. It audits FSL and MRtrix gradient schemes, detects b-vector flip and axis-permutation errors using DWI image evidence, and writes corrected gradient tables with machine-readable provenance. GradLint is designed as a QC gate before diffusion MRI preprocessing, reconstruction, or tractography pipelines. It checks whether the supplied gradient table is geometrically consistent with the diffusion image, reports scheme-quality issues such as shell structure, direction counts, b0 handling, non-unit b-vectors, and angular sampling, and identifies silent convention errors that can otherwise propagate into tensor fitting and tractography results. The core detection method ranks signed axis permutations of the gradient table by a fibre-coherence criterion derived from a diffusion tensor fit. Candidate conventions are evaluated in the appropriate image or world frame for the input format: FSL bvec/bval tables are treated as image-relative, while MRtrix .b tables are treated as world-coordinate gradients. When a high-confidence correction is found, GradLint can emit repaired FSL and/or MRtrix gradient files together with JSON provenance describing the decision, transform, inputs, and outputs.  The software is implemented as a Rust core with thin command-line and Python interfaces. The Python package exposes the same functionality as the CLI and can render JSON reports to Markdown or HTML. Input gradient files are never modified in place unless an explicit overwrite option is used. This record archives the source code for GradLint v1.1.6, corresponding to the GitHub release published on 2026-10-03. The archived source includes the Rust core, CLI, Python bindings, report rendering layer, tests, CI/release metadata, and example materials included in the public source tree. items.summary: This dataset supports the study “A methodological evaluation of deposited-assembly usability and raw-read rescue in a global public Klebsiella pneumoniae genome collection.” It contains accession-level manifests, derived statistical tables, figure-source data, documentation, software-version information, and analysis code supporting an assembly-first workflow with raw-read reconstruction for publicly available sequencing records. Starting from 44,278 geographically resolved eligible records, 1,687 records had no analyzable public genome input, leaving 42,591 records with an analyzable genome input. Of these, two were excluded during final cohort harmonization, resulting in a final analytical collection of 42,589 K. pneumoniae genomes. This collection comprised 40,093 genomes represented by usable public assemblies and 2,496 genomes reconstructed from publicly available sequencing reads. The deposit does not redistribute genome assemblies or raw sequencing reads. Sequence data should be retrieved from the relevant public repositories using the accession identifiers provided in the manifests. The archived materials support reproduction of the post-assembly cohort audit, statistical summaries, and figures. The exact raw-read preprocessing commands used for the rescued genomes were not retained; consequently, adapter-trimming and quality-filtering parameters are not represented as reproducible components of this deposit. Reconstructed and deposited assemblies were nevertheless evaluated using the same post-assembly quality-control criteria before inclusion in the final analytical collection. Jianhua Li and Jing Guo contributed equally to this work. Jing Chen is the corresponding author. Correspondence: dongqingfei@126.com . Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Xiamen Municipality (No. 3502Z202373092).

items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23121305 . This narrative review asks how psychosexual rehabilitation after cancer can be delivered at scale, rather than describing how common sexual dysfunction is. The author organizes the intervention evidence by intensity of care. Low-intensity measures (structured discussion, lubricants and moisturizers, topical lidocaine, brief clinician training) are cheap and reasonably supported. Two widely recommended physical interventions have weaker evidence than assumed: scheduled PDE5 inhibitor "penile rehabilitation" and routine vaginal dilation during radiotherapy. Psychological interventions show small pooled effects, but moderate effects in targeted trials, most clearly therapist-guided internet-based CBT in breast cancer. From this the author proposes a five-step stepped-care model (Steps 0–4, built on extended PLISSIT) with explicit criteria for stepping up and down, plus adaptations for AYA, men on ADT, and sexual and gender minority survivors. The paper moves the field forward by reframing the problem as one of delivery, by challenging two entrenched practices, and by turning scattered evidence into a model that oncology teams, including nurses, could adopt and test. Major issues Methods are not reproducible. The review relies on "targeted searches" with no databases, dates, search terms, or selection process described. Evidence is "appraised qualitatively" with no tool such as GRADE or risk-of-bias assessment. Claims like "strongest trial evidence in breast cancer" may reflect selective sampling. The stepped-care model is not empirically validated. It was derived by the author "mapping" interventions to levels of care, with no consensus process, stakeholder input, or implementation data. The 8–12 week step-up threshold has no cited support. The conclusion that evidence "supports matching intensity to need" goes beyond what the cited studies tested, since none compared stepped care with usual care or direct referral (the paper admits this only at the end). Evidence for Steps 0–2 is mostly clinician-level, not patient-level. The cited training studies show clinicians discuss sexuality more often, not that patient outcomes improve. Yet these steps form the base of the model. Feasibility of nurse- or clinician-delivered care also rests largely on one HSCT trial. Key claims rest on weak or non-peer-reviewed sources. The HSCT multimodal trial [34] is a conference abstract that is called "important for the model." Other supports [28, 47] are also abstracts. Pilot RCTs (23 and 29 couples) underpin the "medium-to-large" couple therapy claims. The paper applies evidence standards inconsistently. It criticizes penile rehabilitation and during-radiotherapy dilation for weak evidence, then recommends supported dilation after radiotherapy based on observational data and an uncontrolled 53-woman cohort (11.5% to 60.9% pre-post), and cites a regimen from an abstract [28]. Inference from pooled versus targeted effects is speculative. The difference (SMD 0.24 vs. d 0.43–0.72) is taken to show that interventions work best when targeted, which supports stepped care. It could equally reflect heterogeneity, study quality, outcome measures, or small-study effects. Effect sizes of different metrics are also compared without confidence intervals. There is no limitations section. It should cover search bias, the breast-cancer skew, scarce data for men, SGM, and LMIC settings, and the lack of cost and workforce evidence. Minor issues PLISSIT is never spelled out, and AYA HOPE is not defined. "Psychosexual rehabilitation" is defined as a staged process but used loosely to include medical and physical treatments. A tighter definition would help. Table 2 level-of-care labels are confusing ("Steps 0–2", "Step 2 (on-demand use)" for a scheduled intervention). The HSCT row gives no sample size. Table 2 says the CBT
items.title: PREreview of "Psychosexual Rehabilitation After Cancer: A Narrative Review of the Intervention Evidence and a Stepped-Care Model for Survivorship Practice"

items.summary: Coordinated multi-humanoid loco-manipulation is promising yet challenging due to high-dimensional whole-body control, decentralized decision making, and scalability. While recent reinforcement learning methods have improved single-humanoid whole-body control, extending them to the multi-humanoid setting remains nontrivial and often requires substantial reward engineering or task-specific design. We propose MASkillBlender, a general multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to achieve decentralized multi-humanoid whole-body coordination. By learning a shared decentralized high-level policy over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills, MASkillBlender enables coordinated behaviors using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references. To improve learning efficiency, we further introduce a permutation-based data augmentation strategy for homogeneous multi-humanoid systems, and theoretically show that the permuted samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples under the homogeneous Markov game formulation. We evaluate MASkillBlender on multiple multi-humanoid coordination tasks across two humanoid embodiments. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves strong task performance and enables coordinated behaviors across different tasks and humanoid embodiments.
items.title: MASkillBlender: Decentralized Whole-Body Coordination for Multi-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Skill Blending

items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: Complete data, code and manuscript for the preprint of the same title. Contains the AlphaFold3 predictions, derived per-sample tables, measured kinetics, analysis code and a self-checking reproduce.py that regenerates every number reported in the paper using the Python standard library alone. Two results. (1) Across 18 non-cognate amino acids, none of three AlphaFold3 confidence observables tracks the published substrate discrimination factors of threonyl-tRNA synthetase (Spearman rho = -0.010, +0.098, -0.028; all p > 0.56); serine, the non-cognate this enzyme rejects best at the binding step, scores highest of all 18 on every observable. (2) The same scores are not blind to the structure: substituting the three zinc-binding residues with alanine collapses the threonine-over-valine preference by 0.112 (95% CI 0.106-0.117) and inverts it, without changing the predicted fold. Combined: the readout is site-sensitive but not affinity-calibrated. Measured discrimination factors are transcribed with attribution from Freist, Sternbach & Cramer (1994) Eur J Biochem 220:745-752, doi:10.1111/j.1432-1033.1994.tb18675.x.
items.title: Structure-prediction confidence detects an enzyme's catalytic site but does not measure how well it discriminates: data, code and manuscript

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).
items.title: Extracting Reproducibility Metadata from Machine-Learning Papers: a Taxonomy of Silent Errors and the Cost of Human Verification

items.summary: The Visibility Problem Hypershape Shadow Hypothesis II   Chloe J. Tully https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332 HSH Paper 1 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23010822 Project UAP Studies   v0.1 3 October 2026 Preprint. Not peer-reviewed.   Companion to HSH I (28 September 2026). Tier-2 material is not in this paper.     DISCIPLINE   HSH I derived a geometry and assumed a flux law. This paper keeps the geometry and splits the assumption. What is proved is proved about the toy model. What is not selected — a coupling, a bulk metric, a relativistic completion — is named and left open. Neural coupling and retrocausality are still excluded. They are not implied by anything below.     ABSTRACT   HSH I predicted a parabolic light curve by taking received flux proportional to the area of the brane slice. That step is not geometry. For a 4-ball translating along the hidden axis, orthographic area scales as ρ² and reproduces the parabola F₂ = 1 − (t/τ)². Uniform emission through the 3-volume of the same slice scales as ρ³ and produces F₃ = [1 − (t/τ)²]^(3/2). The families meet at onset, peak, and end, and disagree in the shoulders: at |t/τ| = 1/√2, F₂ = 1/2 while F₃ = 1/(2√2). Calibrated photometry can tell them apart.   A 4-ellipsoid at fixed orientation in the XW plane stays inside both families, for every line of sight. An orientation that changes during the transit need not. One computed counterexample is given. The C₅ cover twist proposed in open problem O5 — cross-edges (i, 0) ↔ (i+1, 1) in place of the self-steps — is isomorphic to the untwisted cover, so the 1/φ gap is unchanged. No uniform self-step weight puts the even sector on the five-value spectrum flagged in HSH I. Coupling remains the critical open problem. Ansätze are stated with kill criteria. None is adopted.     CONTENTS   1. What HSH I already fixed 2. Two measures, two light curves 3. Fixed orientation stays parabolic 4. The C₅ twist does not close O5 5. Coupling ansätze, none chosen 6. What this does not unlock 7. Status of claims

items.summary: We give an explicit convex polygon with 63 rational vertices whose area, after its shortest closed Euclidean billiard length is normalized to one, is smaller than that of Mallée’s parabolic triangle. This disproves Conjecture 2.2 of Balitskiy, Mitrofanov and Polyanskii (2026). The polygon was found by moving supporting lines near the parabolic triangle’s focal contacts and then discretizing the resulting shape. The proof checks the literal polygon in exact rational arithmetic: 63 width directions and all 39,711 triples of supporting edge lines. A three-file verification package contains the coordinates and an independent checker. The result identifies a better competitor, without claiming that it is optimal.
items.title: A rational polygonal counterexample to the Mallée parabolic triangle conjecture

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.
items.title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

items.summary: Coordinated multi-humanoid loco-manipulation is promising yet challenging due to high-dimensional whole-body control, decentralized decision making, and scalability. While recent reinforcement learning methods have improved single-humanoid whole-body control, extending them to the multi-humanoid setting remains nontrivial and often requires substantial reward engineering or task-specific design. We propose MASkillBlender, a general multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to achieve decentralized multi-humanoid whole-body coordination. By learning a shared decentralized high-level policy over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills, MASkillBlender enables coordinated behaviors using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references. To improve learning efficiency, we further introduce a permutation-based data augmentation strategy for homogeneous multi-humanoid systems, and theoretically show that the permuted samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples under the homogeneous Markov game formulation. We evaluate MASkillBlender on multiple multi-humanoid coordination tasks across two humanoid embodiments. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves strong task performance and enables coordinated behaviors across different tasks and humanoid embodiments.
items.title: MASkillBlender: Decentralized Whole-Body Coordination for Multi-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Skill Blending

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. Kaggle. https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/195341 Official source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (`CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`).

items.summary: CORE-LLM-Bench is a controlled neurosymbolic benchmark for evaluating ontology-grounded reasoning in large language models. Version 1.1.0 contains 9,048 unique question-hop instances derived from four ontology datasets: Family, Pizza 100, Pizza 250, and OWL2Bench. The benchmark contains 6,032 binary question-answering (BQA) instances and 3,016 open-ended question-answering (OEQA) instances. Benchmark instances support 1-hop and 2-hop ontology contexts and aligned natural-language (NL), formal-symbolic (FS), and entity-abstracted (AR) representations. Ground-truth answers and explanation structures are derived using symbolic ontology reasoning, enabling controlled evaluation according to task formulation, representation, semantic abstraction, context depth, explanation-based reasoning complexity, and reasoning type. The release includes benchmark data, reasoning metadata, provenance and licensing documentation, release manifests and checksums, and scripts supporting benchmark generation, validation, Hugging Face export, and reproducibility. The canonical source-code release is CORE-LLM-Bench v1.1.0 on GitHub. Licensing is component-specific. Repository software is MIT licensed; separable original CORE-LLM-Bench benchmark content is CC BY 4.0; Pizza-derived material follows CC BY 3.0; OWL2Bench-derived material follows Apache-2.0; and Family/FHKB-derived material follows CC BY-SA 3.0. See NOTICE.md for detailed provenance, attribution, and modification information.

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23121295 . This narrative review asks how psychosexual rehabilitation after cancer can be delivered at scale, rather than describing how common sexual dysfunction is. The author organizes the intervention evidence by intensity of care. Low-intensity measures (structured discussion, lubricants and moisturizers, topical lidocaine, brief clinician training) are cheap and reasonably supported. Two widely recommended physical interventions have weaker evidence than assumed: scheduled PDE5 inhibitor "penile rehabilitation" and routine vaginal dilation during radiotherapy. Psychological interventions show small pooled effects, but moderate effects in targeted trials, most clearly therapist-guided internet-based CBT in breast cancer. From this the author proposes a five-step stepped-care model (Steps 0–4, built on extended PLISSIT) with explicit criteria for stepping up and down, plus adaptations for AYA, men on ADT, and sexual and gender minority survivors. The paper moves the field forward by reframing the problem as one of delivery, by challenging two entrenched practices, and by turning scattered evidence into a model that oncology teams, including nurses, could adopt and test. Major issues Methods are not reproducible. The review relies on "targeted searches" with no databases, dates, search terms, or selection process described. Evidence is "appraised qualitatively" with no tool such as GRADE or risk-of-bias assessment. Claims like "strongest trial evidence in breast cancer" may reflect selective sampling. The stepped-care model is not empirically validated. It was derived by the author "mapping" interventions to levels of care, with no consensus process, stakeholder input, or implementation data. The 8–12 week step-up threshold has no cited support. The conclusion that evidence "supports matching intensity to need" goes beyond what the cited studies tested, since none compared stepped care with usual care or direct referral (the paper admits this only at the end). Evidence for Steps 0–2 is mostly clinician-level, not patient-level. The cited training studies show clinicians discuss sexuality more often, not that patient outcomes improve. Yet these steps form the base of the model. Feasibility of nurse- or clinician-delivered care also rests largely on one HSCT trial. Key claims rest on weak or non-peer-reviewed sources. The HSCT multimodal trial [34] is a conference abstract that is called "important for the model." Other supports [28, 47] are also abstracts. Pilot RCTs (23 and 29 couples) underpin the "medium-to-large" couple therapy claims. The paper applies evidence standards inconsistently. It criticizes penile rehabilitation and during-radiotherapy dilation for weak evidence, then recommends supported dilation after radiotherapy based on observational data and an uncontrolled 53-woman cohort (11.5% to 60.9% pre-post), and cites a regimen from an abstract [28]. Inference from pooled versus targeted effects is speculative. The difference (SMD 0.24 vs. d 0.43–0.72) is taken to show that interventions work best when targeted, which supports stepped care. It could equally reflect heterogeneity, study quality, outcome measures, or small-study effects. Effect sizes of different metrics are also compared without confidence intervals. There is no limitations section. It should cover search bias, the breast-cancer skew, scarce data for men, SGM, and LMIC settings, and the lack of cost and workforce evidence. Minor issues PLISSIT is never spelled out, and AYA HOPE is not defined. "Psychosexual rehabilitation" is defined as a staged process but used loosely to include medical and physical treatments. A tighter definition would help. Table 2 level-of-care labels are confusing ("Steps 0–2", "Step 2 (on-demand use)" for a scheduled intervention). The HSCT row gives no sample size. Table 2 says the CBT
items.title: PREreview of "Psychosexual Rehabilitation After Cancer: A Narrative Review of the Intervention Evidence and a Stepped-Care Model for Survivorship Practice"

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete measured data and the full analysis code for the paper "Direction and scale in secondary-path mismatch: a measurable decomposition of the FxLMS update on real acoustic paths". It comprises (i) measured secondary-path impulse responses and recorded reference and disturbance waveforms from a physical active-noise-control rig, acquired under a nominal condition and four propagation conditions in two re-installation campaigns; (ii) the complete Python analysis pipeline, including descriptor computation, sweep and baseline experiments, spectral diagnostics and figure generation; and (iii) verify_numbers.py, which re-checks every numerical value quoted in the paper against the raw data (335 automated checks). Running "python anc_stage2/verify_numbers.py" from the repository root reproduces the full numerical audit. The archive is restricted during peer review and will be made openly accessible upon acceptance of the paper.  Version 2.0 is the structural revision following the final pre-submission review round: the title reads "measured acoustic paths"; the abstract, highlights and contributions are rewritten around the exact batch one-step descent threshold mu_crit ~ rho/(kappa*lambda_eff) and the positioning of the decomposition as attribution rather than replacement of classical phase diagnostics; the ranking-disagreement counts are reported with double denominators (18/40 cross-condition pairs, equivalently 18/24 among pairs admitting a positive budget; campaign 1: 20/40 = 20/24); the mismatch-sweep table moves to the supplementary material (with the growth-diagnostic column) and a classical per-condition summary table is added to the main text; standard deviations are unified to the sample convention (N-1); the supplementary tables label mu_crit as the algebraic value 2*rho/(n*lambda_eff*kappa). No new experiments; all measured data unchanged. The automated audit is extended to 456 checks. Version 2.1 removes the LaTeX manuscript sources from the archive; data, results and analysis code are unchanged, and the automated audit skips the manuscript-source checks automatically when the sources are absent.
items.title: Data and code for "Direction and scale in secondary-path mismatch: a measurable decomposition of the FxLMS update on measured acoustic paths"

items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms increasingly rely on language-model agents to provide adaptive mission-level reasoning in uncertain environments. Fully distributed control, in which each UAV hosts an independent Small Language Model (SLM), removes reliance on a centralized coordinator but introduces an information-management problem: long-running interaction histories can degrade the reasoning context, while indiscriminate information dissemination increases communication and inference overhead. We address these challenges with a distributed UAV-agent architecture that enables continuous local SLM control through an event-driven reason-act-observe lifecycle. Runtime knowledge is represented as structured atomic notes and organized into core, local, and peer-specific memory. A deterministic interest-aware gossip engine selectively disseminates these notes according to recipient-specific semantic novelty and recency. We evaluate the architecture using ten UAVs in a simulated search-and-rescue mission. Our approach completes all experimental runs, whereas unrestricted flooding messages completes only 70-85\%, and delegating forwarding decisions to the SLM prevents mission completion in every run. Compared with unrestricted flooding, our approach approximately halves inference-token consumption, reduces transmitted data, and achieves lower survivor-count error.
items.title: Managing Context and Communication in Distributed Agentic UAV Swarms

items.summary: This repository provides the compiled analysis inputs, R code, figure source data and GIS rasters supporting the manuscript “Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change”. Version 2.0 contains the final USA-intersection climatic-analogue reconstruction and its corresponding model predictions and spatial summaries. The historical introduction pool contains 18,562 species. The stage-transition models use 5,791 complete-case species, of which 4,088 species without a recorded invasion form the future candidate invasion-debt subset. Future predictions cover 12 combinations of two climate scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585), three periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080 and 2081–2100), and two global climate models (HadGEM3-GC31-LL and MPI-ESM1-2-HR). The archive contains: • Figure_data: XLSX source workbooks for main Figures 1–4, Supplementary Figures S1–S4 and Supplementary Tables S1–S15, together with the compiled species-level analysis dataset and current and future candidate-species predictions. • Code: R scripts, computational inputs and provenance documentation for the stage-transition models, climatic-analogue searches, future predictions, phylogenetic null analysis, temporal analyses, sensitivity analyses and publication source tables. • GIS_rasters: GeoTIFFs for the main and supplementary spatial figures. Main Figure 4 rasters contain sums within globally aligned 0.5° display cells; supplementary spatial rasters retain the native 10-arc-minute resolution. • Validation: execution records and numerical checks. • README files: instructions for reproducing the analyses, plotting the source data and interpreting the spatial fields. Current and future closest US climatic analogue cells are identified separately for each candidate species. POT is the sum of future predicted invasion probabilities assigned to future analogue cells. CHG is future grid-level transition potential minus current grid-level transition potential, with unassigned cells completed with zero. CHG therefore incorporates both changes in predicted probability and relocation of climatic analogues. POSDP is the sum of positive species-level changes assigned to future analogue cells; Supplementary Figure S3 reports its range across the two climate models. The analytical workflow was tested with R 4.3.3. Reproduction starts from the compiled historical master dataset, supplied phylogenetic inputs, prepared species climatic centroids and extracted WorldClim grid values. The package does not independently repeat every upstream archive-curation decision, manual stage-status assignment, GBIF download or occurrence-cleaning step. These boundaries and the optional XLSX and GeoTIFF export procedures are documented in the README. The historical count of 15,950 candidate invasion-debt species is retained for historical summaries; it is not the population used for future predictions. This release supersedes the earlier spatial outputs based on a rectangular climate-search domain. Future results should be interpreted as conditional model projections rather than evidence of a statistically established climate-driven increase in invasion. The repository record is distributed under CC BY 4.0. The software license included in Code/LICENSE and the original terms of third-party inputs remain applicable.
